b: The oldest sustained treatment of the question in Scripture. Job's friends offer the standard answer — suffering is punishment, so repent — and the book declares them wrong. Job demands an explanation and never receives one.

What he receives instead is God himself, in four chapters of questions about creation. The resolution is relational rather than informational, which is either deeply unsatisfying or exactly right depending on where you are when you read it.

1.t: The reader is shown the heavenly scene; Job never is. That asymmetry is the key to the book.
After losing everything, in the same breath as tearing his robe. The narrator adds that in all this Job did not sin.

2.h: Shall we accept good and not trouble
2.t: Job's answer to his wife. The narrator again notes he did not sin in what he said.
Job's friends do their best work before they open their mouths.

38.t: Four chapters of questions about creation, and no explanation of the suffering. What Job receives is not information but God.
When I laid the earth's foundation. God answers a question about suffering with a question about creation.

42.h: I had heard, now I see
42.t: Job repents of what he said, not of what he was accused of. The friends are told they have not spoken rightly, and Job prays for them.
God says they have not spoken rightly, and Job must pray for them. Restoration comes after intercession for the people who wounded him.

3.t: Not God, but the day he was born. The book allows the full weight of that without correcting him.

19.h: I know that my Redeemer lives
19.t: Spoken at the lowest point of the book, not at the resolution. Handel set it; Job had no evidence for it.

23.t: Forward, backward, left, right — and then: but he knows the way that I take. Faith without felt presence.

4.t: Kindly at first, and built on a vision he had at night. His logic — the innocent do not perish — is the assumption the book exists to demolish.

9.h: If only there were a mediator
9.t: Job wishes for someone to lay a hand on them both. The New Testament answers a question Job could only ask.

14.h: If a man dies, will he live again
14.t: Asked, not answered. Job's honesty is what makes the book usable to people in the middle of grief.

28.t: A poem on the inaccessibility of wisdom, ending with the only answer available: the fear of the Lord.

31.t: A remarkable ethical self-examination, including a covenant with his eyes and his treatment of servants and the poor.

40.t: God's second speech asks whether Job would condemn him in order to justify himself. That is the actual charge.

5.h: He wounds but he binds up
5.t: Eliphaz saying something true inside an argument that is wrong. Not every sentence from a bad counsellor is false.

6.h: A despairing man should have the devotion of his friends
6.t: Job's complaint about how he is being treated.

7.t: I will speak out in the anguish of my spirit. Job claims the right to complain.

8.t: Blunter than Eliphaz: your children sinned and God gave them over. Said to a man whose ten children have just died.

10.t: Job argues from being made by God to being owed an explanation by him.

11.h: Can you fathom the mysteries of God
11.t: Zophar asks a good question for the wrong reason, and God asks it again at the end for the right one.

12.h: To God belong wisdom and power
12.t: Job knows the orthodox answers as well as his friends do, and says so.

13.h: Though he slay me, yet will I hope in him
13.t: The Hebrew is difficult and can also read 'I have no hope'. Both renderings are defensible and translations differ. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

16.t: One who pleads for me as a man pleads for his friend. Job keeps reaching for a mediator.

17.t: Short, flat, and without any attempt to soften it.

21.h: Why do the wicked live on
21.t: Job's counter-evidence against his friends' whole system.

27.h: I will not deny my integrity
27.t: Job refuses to confess sins he has not committed in order to fit their theory.

29.h: How I long for the months gone by
29.t: Job remembers respect, usefulness and family. Grief includes the loss of who you were.

30.h: I cry out to you but you do not answer
30.t: The contrast with chapter 29 is the whole point.

32.t: A younger man who waited and then speaks for six chapters. Interpreters divide on whether he is right; notably God neither rebukes nor commends him.

39.t: Mountain goats, the wild donkey, the ostrich, the warhorse, the hawk. Creatures useless to humans, delighted in by God.

41.t: A whole chapter on a creature nobody can control. The argument is cumulative: you cannot manage this, and I made it.

15.t: Sharper this time: Job's own words condemn him. The friends are escalating because Job will not accept their explanation.

18.h: Bildad on the fate of the wicked
18.t: A catalogue of disasters that fall on the ungodly — delivered to a man suffering exactly those disasters.

20.t: The wicked's prosperity is brief. True as a general observation and cruel as an accusation.

22.t: Having no evidence, he supplies it: you must have stripped the naked and refused water to the weary. Theory driving the facts.

24.h: Why does the Almighty not set times
24.t: Job describes the poor exploited while God appears to do nothing. The question is left standing.

25.t: Six verses, and the friends' arguments run out. How can a man be righteous before God? A good question, badly used.

26.t: Job says all creation is only the edge of God's ways, a whisper. He knows God's greatness as well as his friends do.

33.t: Elihu suggests suffering may be God's instruction rather than punishment. Interpreters are divided on whether he advances the argument. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

34.h: Far be it from God to do evil
34.t: Elihu defends God's justice. His conclusion is orthodox; his treatment of Job is harsh.

35.t: People cry out under oppression but do not ask where God is. Elihu names a real failure in how people suffer.

36.h: He delivers the afflicted by their affliction
36.t: A compact statement of how suffering can be used, set in the build-up to God's own speech.

37.t: Elihu ends with the storm — the very storm from which God is about to speak.
